site.title: things i've built
site.tagline: built with Claude Code, and used every day
site.name: Andy Keeley

intro:
I'm a commercial leader, not a developer. In February I started building with Claude Code, on the view that the tools had quietly become good enough for someone who understands the problem to build the fix themselves. Seven months on, some of it runs my working week and some of it runs the house. Most of it I use every day. The hard part was never the code. It was describing the problem properly, arguing with the output until it was right, and then actually using it.

At home, my kids have worked out that if they can describe it, we can build it.
introAside: And, of course, this website was built in a couple of hours with a dollop of vision and a few good prompts.

projects.name: mentor-agent
projects.strapline: A chief of staff with an IQ of 140, sitting on my shoulder.
bullets: Connected to Gmail, Google Calendar and the EOS rocks store
Structured memory in plain files: a handover from the last session, a lessons file of its own mistakes, GTD, the pipeline, one file per customer, a knowledge base and a daily journal
One-letter commands and skills, so capturing something or checking the week costs nothing
Rituals it runs with me: every morning, every Friday, and before every negotiation
What comes out: today's plan, deal prep briefs, drafts, boards and design briefs
projects.outcome: Not a chatbot. A system that knows my inbox, calendar, pipeline and customers.

value.tip: genuinely can't work without it now

projects.name: sorry-quick-q
projects.strapline: Every school letter, newsletter, WhatsApp forward and noticeboard photo in one deployed AI. Ask it anything.
projects.description: A knowledge base built from the boys' school comms — letters, newsletters, WhatsApp forwards, photos of a noticeboard — answering "what kit does he need Thursday?" at 7am, instead of asking the group chat. School comms constantly overwrite themselves, so nothing is ever deleted: new facts supersede old ones, but only if the source outranks what it replaces — a parent's forward can't retire the school's own letter. Citations resolve by ID so the model can't invent a source, and "I don't know" is a first-class answer.

effort.tip: two repos, and a week of arguing about supersession

value.tip: answers it before i have to ask the group chat

projects.name: investment-agent
projects.strapline: An autonomous trading agent, live on Kraken with real money, whose rules are rewritten from its own trade history.
projects.description: Autonomous trading agent. Scans the crypto market, scores candidates on momentum, sentiment, risk/reward and liquidity, sizes the position through a risk manager, executes on Kraken, and emails me a daily digest of what it did and why. The interesting part isn't the trading — it's the rules it can't talk itself out of: stop-loss set at entry, a hard cash floor, a maximum hold it has to re-underwrite. Runs unattended.

effort.tip: weekends and evenings over ~3 weeks, still tuning

bullets: Scans the Kraken market and scores every candidate on momentum, sentiment, risk/reward and liquidity
A separate risk manager sizes every trade before anything executes
Stop-loss set at entry, half banked at +8%, a cash floor it can't breach, and a maximum hold it has to re-justify
Every trade logged with its reasoning, and a daily email of what it did and why
The rules change when the data says so: the profit target moved from +15% to +8% once it was clear no trade had ever reached +15%

projects.name: fitness-mentor
projects.strapline: A coach that remembers every session: annual and quarterly goals, the training block, injury rehab, and a phone app for the gym.
projects.description: My coach, and a continuous conversation rather than a one-off plan. Annual and quarterly goals, a training block that serves them, and injury rehab with its own progression ladder. Before it does anything else it runs the arithmetic on my own data and tells me what's drifted: a skipped session, rehab that isn't going in, or a block that quietly finished and needs re-planning. The session lands on a phone app before I get to the gym, and it wrote the brief I took to my physio.

effort.tip: restructured twice as i worked out what i needed

value.tip: replaced a coach i was paying for

projects.name: anki-srs
projects.strapline: Spaced repetition built properly, for paintings, capitals and commercial fundamentals.
projects.description: Spaced repetition built properly — SM-2 scheduling, four-button grading, and an append-only review log so I can swap the algorithm out later without losing history. Card types are pluggable, so one deck of famous paintings became decks for capitals, flags, US states, life philosophies and commercial fundamentals.

effort.tip: a weekend, then kept extending it

value.tip: the commercial deck earns its keep

projects.name: health-tracker
projects.strapline: Garmin sleep, heart rate and HRV, set against how I actually live.
projects.description: Pulls resting heart rate, HRV and sleep score straight from Garmin, and sets them against a simple daily log of lifestyle factors: exercise, travel, late caffeine, a night out. Insights come with a confidence level and a sample size, so it only tells me what the data can actually support. Plus charts, streaks and a history view.

projects.name: outreach board
projects.strapline: A job search run like a sales pipeline: every contact scored, staged, and with a clear view of whose move it is.
bullets: Every person and role scored on desire × winnability, so the list doesn't quietly reorder itself around whatever's available
Stages with a definition, not a feeling: "warm" means they advocate for you without being asked
Whose move it is flips automatically when a chase date passes
A weekly scorecard where the only leading indicator is conversations opened
projects.outcome: No warm lead goes cold because nobody noticed it was my move.

value.tip: treats my own pipeline the way i'd treat a customer's

projects.name: commercial toolkit
projects.strapline: The commercial jobs I used to do by hand: RFPs, negotiation prep, the deal board, CRM hygiene and customer health.
bullets: RFP builder: first-pass answers drafted from everything we've written before, with sources, and gaps left blank for a human
Deal prep: a questioning agent that won't produce a brief until the value case, leverage, objections and ask are credible
Deal sprint board: five gates per deal, with readiness calculated from the prep, never hand-set
Customer health: one score per account, straight into the board pack
HubSpot sync: CRM kept in line with the working pipeline (retired when the book got small)
projects.outcome: Each one took a recurring commercial job and made it faster and more consistent.

effort.tip: five tools, none of them a weekend

value.tip: the jobs still happen, just properly

usage.tip: whenever a bid, a negotiation or a board pack lands

projects.name: zenbox
projects.strapline: Sorts my Gmail on rules I control, with a Chrome extension to change them in place, and replaced a paid subscription.
projects.description: Self-hosted email triage that replaced a paid SaneBox subscription. Gmail pushes new mail through Pub/Sub to a service that sorts it on rules I control — whitelist, greylist, am-I-actually-a-recipient, bulk-mail detection. Two independent instances, one per mailbox, sharing only the code. Plus a Chrome extension so I can change a sender's rule without leaving the inbox.

value.tip: cancelled the subscription, kept the quiet inbox

projects.name: hotel booking engine

bullets: Search, results, rooms, basket and book, end to end
Built on our own Universal Hotel API, not a mock
My first real build, made to start a conversation with the engineering team
projects.outcome: Their reaction was the whole point. It has moved on a lot since this demo.

effort.tip: my first real build, steep learning curve

value.tip: proved the concept to the team

projects.name: maths-challenge
projects.strapline: Maths practice for two nine-year-olds, disguised as a fighting game.
projects.description: Maths practice for my boys, disguised as a fighting game. Eight Key Stage 2 topics; each round is a match against an opponent with a health bar, a super meter that rewards streaks, and a rank stamp at the end. Nothing in it reads as losing — that was a design rule. There's a second area of trials modelled on their school's cognitive assessment. The save file has no reset button, on purpose: their history is the only record of what they've played, and the only input for tuning the difficulty.

effort.tip: the most iterated thing i've built

projects.name: sonic-fighters
projects.strapline: A 3D fighting game in the browser, made for my boys.
projects.description: A browser fighting game for my boys. Three.js, a physically-based rendering pipeline, a night arena and a broadcast-style HUD. Started as a weekend thing, then got rebuilt from the visuals up once they kept asking for more characters.

effort.tip: rebuilt once i knew what good looked like

projects.name: beyblade-clash
projects.strapline: A Beyblade battle in the browser, built in an evening because they asked.
projects.description: Two-to-three player Beyblade battle in the browser. Spin physics, collisions, stadium walls, hand-drawn bey art. Built in an evening because they asked.

projects.name: wordle-solver
projects.strapline: One of my first builds, as a test: it suggests the guess that rules out the most answers. Try not to cheat.
projects.description: One of my first projects, and a test of the idea more than something I use. It works over the official answer list: feed it what you know and it suggests the guess that eliminates the most remaining possibilities. Deployed, so anyone can use it.
